title: How Has Consumerism Shaped American Christianity?
subtitle: How consumerism, comfort, and the market have shaped the church more than the cross
question: We are quick to name the captivities we can see in other people. The tribe that votes the other way. The nation that flatters itself. The culture that has lost its way. But there is a captivity that does not announce itself, because it feels like rest. It feels like blessing. The question is whether the market has discipled us more deeply than the gospel, and whether we would even know it if it had.
whyItMatters: Most captivities arrive as force. This one arrives as comfort, which is why it is the hardest to repent of. A persecuted church knows its chains. A comfortable church mistakes its chains for furniture. We have built sanctuaries that function as showrooms, sermons that perform as self-help, and a faith calibrated to the felt needs of the religious consumer who can take his attendance elsewhere if the experience disappoints. We did not decide this in a council. We absorbed it the way a sponge absorbs water, slowly, without resistance, until the shape of the church matched the shape of the mall.
biblicalFoundation:
A man with everything came to Jesus and asked what he still lacked. He was rich, devout, sincere. Jesus did not soften the answer to keep him in the room. Go, sell what you have, and come follow me. The man went away grieving, because he had great possessions, and Jesus let him go. This is the only place in the Gospels where someone asks to follow and Jesus raises the price instead of lowering it. We have spent two thousand years finding ways to say he did not really mean it.

Jesus drew the line without apology. No one can serve two masters. You cannot serve God and Mammon. He did not say it is difficult to serve both. He said it is impossible, and he named money as a rival god, a power that demands worship and rewards loyalty and punishes defection. The market is not neutral. It catechizes. It tells us who we are by what we can afford, and it offers a liturgy of acquisition that runs every hour of every day in the background of our attention.

In the parable of the sower, the seed that falls among thorns is choked not by persecution but by the cares of the world and the deceitfulness of riches. Note the word deceitful. Wealth lies. It promises a security it cannot give and a peace it cannot keep, and it does its work quietly, on people who would never describe themselves as greedy. The seed does not die in a storm. It is strangled in a garden.

And to the church at Laodicea, the church that said I am rich, I have prospered, I need nothing, the risen Christ said the hardest words in the book. You do not know that you are wretched, pitiable, poor, blind, and naked. This is the church that thought its prosperity was proof of God's favor, and it is the only church Jesus threatened to spit out of his mouth. Lay not up for yourselves treasures on earth. We read it. We frame it. We have not believed it.
keyTexts: Matthew 6:24 (you cannot serve God and Mammon)
Mark 4:18-19 (the deceitfulness of riches choking the seed)
Matthew 6:19-21 (do not store up treasures on earth)
Luke 12:15 (a man's life does not consist in possessions)

churchRecord.led: There have always been those who saw it and walked out of it. The desert fathers who fled the comforts of empire. Francis stripping himself of his father's wealth in the public square. The Methodist class meetings that asked working people to account for every shilling. Bonhoeffer, who named cheap grace as grace we bestow on ourselves, grace without discipleship, grace without the cross. In every age a remnant has refused to let the faith be furnished.
churchRecord.failed: More often the church has blessed the captivity instead of breaking it. It baptized the slave economy that funded its steeples. It preached a prosperity that made God a vendor and the believer a customer. It built ministry on the techniques of marketing and called the result growth. It measured faithfulness in attendance and offering and square footage, and it learned to fear the empty seat more than it feared the Lord. We have been very good at building. We have been less good at counting the cost.

whereWeAgree: Across the divisions of the church, almost no one defends greed by name. We all confess that the love of money is a root of evil and that comfort can dull the soul. The agreement is loud. It is the obedience that is quiet.
captureLeft: A comfortable progressive Christianity can domesticate the faith by trading the cross for a politics of self-actualization, where grace asks nothing it has not already affirmed and the gospel becomes a chaplain to a lifestyle already chosen. It keeps the language of justice and quietly drops the call to die.
captureRight: A comfortable consumer Christianity domesticates the faith just as thoroughly by treating church as a product, worship as an experience to be rated, and the believer as a sovereign customer whose preferences set the terms. It keeps the language of conviction and quietly drops the cost.
whereWeDiffer: The two captivities will argue endlessly about which worldliness is worse, each certain it has resisted the temptation it cannot see in itself. The honest answer is that both have made peace with comfort and called it conviction. The market does not care which side wins the argument, because it has already sold to both.
theCost: To break this captivity costs the one thing we are least willing to spend, which is comfort itself. It means treasure given away that could have been kept, status risked that could have been protected, a life measured by a cross instead of a balance sheet. The rich man went away grieving for a reason. The price was real.
charge: We will not be persecuted out of this one. No empire will come for the comfortable church, because the comfortable church threatens no empire. The chains are soft, and they are warm, and they are ours, and I am writing this from inside them. The question Jesus left hanging over the rich young ruler still hangs over us, unanswered, every Sunday, in every padded pew. He let the man walk away sad rather than follow him cheap. The text does not tell us whether the man ever came back. It does not tell us whether we will either.

right.label: The Consumer Church
right.whatItLooksLike: On this side the captivity wears the clothes of growth and excellence. The church is built as a product with a coffee bar in the lobby, a parking ministry to ease the arrival, and a worship set engineered to move a crowd from anticipation to release. The believer is treated as a sovereign customer whose felt needs set the agenda, and the cross becomes one feature among many in a faith marketed as personal enhancement.
right.inThePast: The seeker-sensitive movement built at Willow Creek Community Church under Bill Hybels in the 1970s and after applied consumer research to the unchurched, designing services around the preferences of a man the planners called Unchurched Harry. Robert Schuller preached possibility thinking from the Crystal Cathedral and told pastors to think of the church as a retail business meeting consumer needs. The Church Growth movement that traced back to Donald McGavran and was carried forward at Fuller Seminary by C. Peter Wagner made numerical increase a measurable science. Rick Warren codified the model for tens of thousands of congregations through The Purpose Driven Church.
right.now: In 2018 Willow Creek itself published the Reveal study, which found that programming attendance did not reliably produce spiritual maturity, an admission from inside the movement that the metrics had measured the wrong thing. The prosperity gospel associated with figures such as Joel Osteen and Kenneth Copeland turned God into a vendor and faith into a strategy for return. Multi-site and broadcast churches now run worship as a rated experience, and the language of branding, customer experience, and attendance analytics has become ordinary in church management circles.
named: Willow Creek and the seeker-sensitive model

left.label: The Comfortable Progressive
left.whatItLooksLike: On this side the captivity wears the clothes of conscience and inclusion. The radicalism is verbal and the cost is rhetorical, a faith that keeps the vocabulary of justice while asking nothing the congregation has not already decided to give. Spirituality becomes therapeutic and curated, a practice of affirmation in which grace confirms the self rather than crucifying it.
left.inThePast: The sociologist Robert Bellah and his coauthors in Habits of the Heart in 1985 named the figure of Sheila, who described her private religion as Sheilaism, a faith of one. Christian Smith and the National Study of Youth and Religion in 2005 documented Moralistic Therapeutic Deism, a creed in which God wants people to be nice and happy and stays mostly out of the way. Philip Rieff in The Triumph of the Therapeutic in 1966 had already traced the replacement of the believer who sacrifices with the consumer who seeks well-being. Affluent mainline and progressive congregations long combined comfortable circumstances with the language of prophetic critique.
left.now: The rise of those who claim to be spiritual but not religious, tracked in Pew Research Center surveys, marks a boutique spirituality assembled from preference. Wellness culture has absorbed religious practice into self-care, with meditation apps and curated retreats selling interior calm as a product. Progressive congregations can pass resolutions on justice while their own wealth, real estate, and patterns of life remain untouched, and the call to die to self quietly drops out while the moral language stays.
named: Sheilaism in Habits of the Heart
